title: The path of dhamma
hookLine: a collection of the Buddha's verses, beloved across the Buddhist world (Dhammapada)
tomorrow: if everyone dies, why does it say the earnest never do?

lines: COFFEE ON THE FLOOR. DID THEY MEAN IT?
A BLIND MONK, A RAINY NIGHT.
cards: A stranger bumps your arm on the train and your coffee hits the floor. Before anyone says sorry, you're already reading their face: did they mean it? That snap read of intent is where the Dhammapada begins.
Its very first line, in Max Müller's translation: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." Mind first.
And Buddhist tradition hangs a story on that line, about a blind monk, a rainy night, and a path covered in insects.

teach.h: A BLIND MONK ON A RAINY PATH.
teach.b: The Dhammapada is a small book of the Buddha's verses, and its old commentary gives each verse a story. The first belongs to an elder named Cakkhupala.
Tradition says he vowed to spend a rainy season without lying down, only walking and sitting in meditation. His eyes failed, and he kept walking.

One night after rain, insects swarmed onto his walking path, and he crushed them without seeing. In the morning, visiting monks found the bodies and went to the Buddha: this monk is killing living things.
The Buddha asked: did you see him kill them? No. Neither did he.
He had no thought of killing, so there was no fault. Then the verses. The first chapter is the Twin-Verses, lines in pairs.
Act with an evil thought, and "pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage." Act with a pure thought, and happiness follows like a shadow.
So the teaching: in Buddhism, karma is intention. In another sutta the Buddha says it outright: intention is what he calls karma.
That's why Buddhists start with the mind, and why the same act can weigh differently depending on what was meant. It isn't think-positive. A smile over a cruel plan still pulls the cart.
One more thing worth telling a friend: some readers take the title two ways, verses of dhamma or the path of dhamma, hearing pada as a line or as a step.

how: Buddhists in many countries read, chant and memorize verses of the Dhammapada; teachers often tell the commentary's story behind a verse before explaining it.

games.q: what does “the path of dhamma” mean?
o: the Buddha's verses, read as steps on a path
a list of the Buddha's past lives and births
a Buddhist rulebook for monks and nuns only

games.q: the first verse and its story: tap the pairs.
p: the blind elder on the walking path
crushed unseen, with no thought to kill
follows the ox, as pain follows evil thought
the first chapter, lines in pairs

s: the Dhammapada's first line is about the mind
all that we are is the result of what we have thought.
the first verse means: think positive and good things come
it's about intention: what you mean to do pulls the cart, not a mood you put on.
the Buddha blamed the blind monk for the insects
he hadn't seen them and had no thought of killing, so there was no fault.

games.q: you're one of the visiting monks. you found the crushed insects on the blind elder's path and told the Buddha. what does he say?
o: he has broken the rule, and he must make amends at once.
did you see him kill them? neither did he. no intention, no fault.
insects are too small to count; only harm to people matters.
games.why: the Buddha looked at the mind: Cakkhupala never meant to kill. that's why the book's first line puts the mind first.

practice: Rest your hands in your lap. Before you move one finger, notice the wish to move it, then let the finger lift and settle. Do it a few times, slowly, catching the intention each time before the motion.
Then let the hands rest, and stay quiet for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The path of dhamma: the Dhammapada, the Buddha's verses, where each line is a step and the first step is the mind.

orig.note: Pali, written in Devanagari: the book's name. some readers take it as verses of dhamma, others as the path of dhamma.

carryVoice: For the road: the path, with the mind walking first on it. The Dhammapada is open.
